title: Vendor Risk Assessment Guide: How to Choose the Right Security & Compliance Platform
description: Practical vendor risk assessment guidance with decision criteria, risk controls, implementation checks, and a readiness checklist.
author: Marcus Rivera

sections.title: Create a vendor inventory
sections.body: List the vendors and services that handle business data, support critical workflows, or can access production systems. Record the business owner, purpose, data types, access level, renewal date, subprocessors, and impact if the service is unavailable or compromised. Include free tools and embedded features, not only signed enterprise contracts. Prioritize assessment depth by risk rather than applying the same questionnaire to every supplier.

sections.title: Classify risk and define evidence
sections.body: Rate the potential impact of data exposure, service outage, supply-chain compromise, and regulatory failure. Decide which evidence is required for each risk tier: security documentation, independent audit reports, penetration-test summaries, privacy terms, recovery results, or a technical demonstration. Record the date and scope of each document. A certification is useful evidence but does not prove that every product, plan, or configuration meets your requirements.

sections.title: Review data handling and privacy
sections.body: Map what data the vendor receives, why it is needed, where it is processed, how long it is retained, and which subprocessors may access it. Review deletion, export, breach notification, international transfer, and contract termination terms. Confirm whether the vendor uses customer data to train or improve other services. Ask the privacy or legal owner to resolve jurisdiction-specific questions instead of treating a questionnaire as legal approval.

sections.title: Assess identity and technical access
sections.body: Check SSO, MFA, role-based permissions, administrator separation, audit logs, secret handling, API scopes, and support access. Identify whether the vendor can reach production systems or customer data and how that access is approved and revoked. For integrations, use scoped credentials and test rotation. Confirm how the vendor notifies you about security incidents, material product changes, and changes to subprocessors.

sections.title: Evaluate resilience and incident response
sections.body: Review service availability commitments, backup and recovery arrangements, business continuity, incident communications, and dependency concentration. Ask for evidence that recovery procedures are exercised. Define your own fallback if the vendor is unavailable or must be disabled quickly. A contract SLA alone does not establish that your business process can recover within its required time.

sections.title: Track remediation and residual risk
sections.body: Record each finding with severity, owner, due date, evidence needed to close it, and the person who can accept remaining risk. Do not leave a critical issue as a note in a spreadsheet without a decision. Establish exception expiry dates and reassessment triggers such as a new data type, product integration, acquisition, or major security incident.

sections.title: Monitor throughout the relationship
sections.body: Set review cadence based on risk and contract length. Track changes to access, data flows, certifications, subprocessors, pricing, service status, and renewal terms. Ensure vendor offboarding includes access revocation, credential rotation, data export or deletion, and termination of integrations. Reassess suppliers when their role changes, not only when the annual questionnaire arrives.

sections.title: Assessment checklist
sections.body: Before onboarding, verify the vendor's purpose, data access, security controls, privacy terms, resilience, incident process, and exit plan. Keep the evidence and decision in a central register with a named business owner. This guide supports risk review but does not replace specialized security testing or legal advice for high-impact engagements.
